items.title: F-35 Readiness Surged in Epic Fury; Now Pentagon and Lockheed Eye Broader Gains
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: For years, sustainment challenges and spare parts shortages have hindered the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter’s readiness. The post F-35 Readiness Surged in Epic Fury; Now Pentagon and Lockheed Eye Broader Gains appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —For years, sustainment challenges and spare parts shortages have hindered the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter’s readiness . But the Air Force’s experience flying F-35s heavily in operations against Iran have showed what the jet can be capable of, if maintainers get all the supplies and support they need.

Brig. Gen. Brian Laidlaw, director of operations for Air Combat Command, said during a Sept. 14 panel discussion at AFA’s Air Space & Cyber conference that the F-35 “absolutely proved itself” during Operation Epic Fury—and keeping a steady flow of spare parts was critical .

“When properly resourced, we showed without a doubt how well this airplane can perform in combat,” Laidlaw said. “When we send our aircraft into harm’s way and they go downrange, they enjoy a higher priority for spare parts and all the things that the logistics trail can get to them. What we saw is how remarkably well the F-35 airplane withstood and maintained really high mission capable rates over a long period of time in the toughest of combat situations.”

The challenge now facing the Air Force, F-35 prime contractor Lockheed Martin, and other parts of the Joint Strike Fighter enterprise: how to keep that level of readiness up, even for aircraft not on the front lines of combat?

A Government Accountability Office report released this June made clear the F-35’s readiness woes are still an issue—just one in four U.S. jets were considered “fully mission capable,” or ready to carry out all their missions at any given time, in fiscal 2025. The Air Force’s full mission capability rate was highest of all U.S. services at 28.5 percent, while the Navy and Marine Corps’ F-35s ranged between 15.3 to 22 percent.

The GAO report cited multiple problems, including spare parts shortages and the military’s decision years ago to prioritize buying more F-35s early in the program’s life cycle instead of investing in critical depot and repair capability. That choice led to a historic underinvestment in sustainment, GAO officials said, that has resulted in a sustainment system that can’t fully support the F-35 fleet.

Yet recent development have shown the Air Force’s larger sustainment enterprise kicking into high gear. In his keynote address Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink continued to harp on the importance of readiness, a frequent theme in his tenure, and said targeted campaigns such as the North Star Readiness Campaign for bombers is helping improve aircraft availability.

During Operation Epic Fury, Meink said, sustainment centers surged procurement of parts by nearly 120 percent to keep aircraft flying. Contractors have also spent billions of their own dollars to stock up on parts military aircraft need, he said.

“The result: our fleet health is showing meaningful progress,” Meink said. “And with Congress’ support, we’ll follow that up with record-high spare parts investment in the next year, and years to come.”

For the F-35 in particular, Dina Halvorsen, vice president of F-35 global sustainment at Lockheed Martin, pointed to several steps the company and the U.S. military have taken to turn around the fighter’s lagging availability in a briefing with reporters at the conference.

In early 2024, Halvorsen said, Lockheed and the F-35 Joint Program Office teamed up to create a “joint model” that spelled out what kind of parts, and how many, would be needed to make F-35s 80 percent mission capable—able to carry out at least one mission—and 65 percent full mission capable.

“It had become very clear that jointly, we [Lockheed and the military] had underinvested in sustainment for the number of jets that we had and flight hours that we wanted to fly,” Halvorsen said.

The team spent about 18 months working on that model, she said, and when it was ready in late summer 2025,, Lockheed made its first $1 billion investment in spare parts.

“We knew what parts were needed, and we didn’t want to wait another year, which is the cycle it would take to get through a congressional budget and get that funding aligned,” Halvorsen said.

Buying that first tranche of spare parts cut out nine or 10 months of lead time, Halvorsen said—and started to position the F-35 for the intense pace of operations that 2026 would bring. Flight hours on all F-35s worldwide are up 25 percent year over year, Halvorsen said, which she said is “putting even more stress on the system.”

But that major infusion of cash didn’t solve everything.

“With all the work we did to buy those initial parts, we realized there were some capacity gaps within the supply chain,” Halvorsen said. “So I could go buy parts, but I wasn’t going to get them in time.”

So Lockheed invested another $1 billion to try to fill that shortfall, Halvorsen said, and figure out what critical components it needed to invest in. That led to a second tranche of spare parts purchases, she said.

In July, the F-35 Joint Program Office awarded Lockheed a record $1.6 billion contract for critical spare parts, which Halvorsen said “liquidated” some of the first tranche of parts Lockheed had bought.

Halvorsen also said Lockheed plans to do more advanced procurement of spare parts to be ready for 2027 and further shrink supply times. That kind of buy-ahead is needed to fully engage the vast array of subcontractors that make F-35 parts, she said—and shows why multiyear purchase agreements for both production and sustainment are so important for the fighter.

“We’re going to keep the supply chain engaged, because to build the capacity, you have to have the demand,” Halvorsen said. “So if you don’t put your total demand into the supply chain, they will never build to the capacity that you need. … We think it’ll drive down overall cost, because if you buy year-to-year, you’re certainly paying for that sort of thing.”

items.title: CMSAF to Airmen: Use AI or ‘End Up in Everyone’s Rearview Mirror’
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Today’s Airmen are going to have to embrace artificial intelligence the same way Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David R. Wolfe learned to love desktop computers and email in the 1990s, the senior enlisted Airman said Sept. 14 during AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. The post CMSAF to Airmen: Use AI or ‘End Up in Everyone’s Rearview Mirror’ appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —Today’s Airmen are going to have to embrace artificial intelligence the same way Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David R. Wolfe learned to love desktop computers and email in the 1990s, the senior enlisted Airman said Sept. 14 during AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.

Wolfe has taken a strong stance on the advantages AI will offer the the Air Force and Airmen of all ranks at a time when much of society remains skeptical over how much control to give the rapidly advancing technology.

“We must overcome this fear if we’re going to fully realize the power of AI,” Wolfe said. “If you choose not to use AI, you are going to end up in everyone’s rearview mirror. … Artificial intelligence will not replace the judgment, discipline, or ingenuity of Airmen, but it can help us see farther down the track, anticipate problems sooner, and make better decisions at the speed the future will demand.”

Wolfe added that the creation of AI isn’t much different from the creation of personal computers and email, innovations he had to learn to adapt to more than 30 years ago.

“When I was given my first email address, honestly, I was skeptical,” Wolfe said, describing how he questioned, “where does this go when I hit send? How do I know who got to the right person? How do I know this is safe?”

“The questions felt pretty reasonable at the time,” he added. “I also thought my leadership was crazy when they told me every desk would soon have a computer on it, but I was wrong. Technology kept moving. We had to learn it, understand it, and figure out how to use it responsibly.”

Shortly after becoming CMSAF late last year, Wolfe stood up an AI Action Team that initially started with 40 members.

“Today we sit at over 200; we brought Airmen together from across the Air Force and asked them to take real problems they understood and see where AI could help,” Wolfe said, adding that the team is “completely rank agnostic” and that the most influential members are often junior Airmen.

Wolfe previously said in May that the service is developing a new training program to ensure every Airman is educated on how to use AI in their everyday job, just weeks after the Air Force released its artificial intelligence strategy .

Noting that he understands the general skepticism around AI, Wolfe said his goal is to reduce the fear many Airmen have of using AI, primarily broken down between two camps: those who worry that AI makes mistakes, and those that fear AI will replace them.

To the former, Wolfe said, “my response is ‘Well, sometimes, so are you.’”

To the latter, Wolfe said, “we’re in an age where that kind of learning is going to be taking place, and the machines are going to be able to make the decisions sometimes at a higher success rate than we will.”

But he stressed that “these capabilities are going to be additive at this point.”

Eventually, Wolfe said, AI may automate enough tasks that leaders can repurpose manpower “to do something else that only humans can do,’’ adding “Why wouldn’t we do that?”

“We’re going to have to make decisions like that sometime in the future,” he said. “But I think it’ll be it’ll be additive as we go on. Think of AI as an increase to the manpower in your units, folks.”

Wolfe encouraged Airmen to let AI allow them “to imagine solutions that were previously unavailable because of human limitations.”

“Technology will keep moving, just like it did when computers and email started showing up on our desks,” Wolfe said. “Our choice is whether we learn fast enough to move with it.”

items.title: Alaska Army National Guard rescues injured mountain biker near Girdwood
items.author: Dana Rosso
items.summary: Alaska Army National Guard aviators rescued an injured mountain biker from the Winner Creek Trail near Girdwood, Sept. 13, after the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center received a request for assistance from the Alaska State Troopers. An HH-60M medevac Black Hawk helicopter and crew assigned to G Company, 2nd Battalion, 211th General Support Aviation Battalion, Alaska Army National Guard, responded to the mission to evacuate the injured biker.
items.body: Alaska Army National Guard aviators rescued an injured mountain biker from the Winner Creek Trail near Girdwood, Sept. 13, after the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center received a request for assistance from the Alaska State Troopers. An HH-60M medevac Black Hawk helicopter and crew assigned to G Company, 2nd Battalion, 211th General Support Aviation Battalion, Alaska Army National Guard, responded to the mission to evacuate the injured biker. Girdwood Fire Department and Alaska Mountain Rescue Group personnel responded on the ground and prepared the patient for aerial evacuation. The ground teams provided the aircrew with an accurate location and prepared the patient for the hoist rescue before the Black Hawk arrived. The HH-60 aircrew located the patient in brush and mountainous terrain along the Winner Creek Trail and used the aircraft’s hoist to safely bring the patient aboard. “The coordination between the RCC, Girdwood Fire Department, the Alaska Mountain Rescue Group and our aircrew and flight medics was outstanding,” said Chief Warrant Officer 3 Mike Miller, pilot in command. “The ground teams gave us great coordinates and had the patient perfectly prepared when we arrived, which allowed us to quickly bring the patient aboard the aircraft.” After the rescue, the aircrew transported the patient to Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage and transferred the patient to hospital medical personnel for follow-on care.

items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The Air Force has erected an inert version of its LGM-35A Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., the service announced Sept. 14.

Officials also confirmed at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that they still expect to finish restructuring the long-troubled Sentinel program by the end of the year and conduct a first test launch in 2027.

The announcement did not specify when the vertical stacking was completed but said that it showed “the maturity of the missile’s design and verified that all critical subsystems are on track.”

An accompanying image shows the missile with “US AIR FORCE” running vertically down its side, along with the Air Force roundel and the emblems of Air Force Global Strike Command and the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center.

In its own announcement, contractor Northrop Grumman said the stacking was a four-month test process that involved transporting missile components “on specially designed vehicles from across the U.S.” to Vandenberg, where technicians “rigorously tested mechanical operations including transportation, mobile crane use, and safe vertical integration while validating all interface connections on the test pad.”

The successful stacking “proved the viability of all missile stages, propulsion elements, shroud, and subcomponents to be assembled into a single configuration on the test pad,” both Northrop and the Air Force said in their releases.

The service has tested the different stages of the Sentinel’s solid rocket motor multiple times in recent years, as well as the new reentry vehicle that will sit atop them. But it has yet to put them all together for a single test of the entire system.

The Air Force also said that its 719th Test Squadron used the stacking event to complete its first “flight test design review” of the Sentinel to ensure it meets requirements for “performance, safety, and mission assurance ahead of flight testing.”

This February, officials announced they were targeting 2027 for the first test launch. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink confirmed in his keynote address at Air, Space & Cyber that the 2027 timeframe still holds.

Holding steady represents a win for the program; in 2024, officials were hoping for a first launch in early 2026. But massive cost and schedule overruns forced the program to restructure and slowed progress, leading the Government Accountability Office in 2025 to project a first launch in March 2028.

Gen. Dale R. White, director of critical major weapons systems, is overseeing Sentinel as the program tries to rebuild momentum from those overruns, which triggered a congressional notification and a Pentagon review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act.

As part of that process, Pentagon leaders rescinded Sentinel’s Milestone B decision, which authorizes officials to work on engineering and manufacturing development. Program leaders were instructed to restructure to manage the cost growth and schedule slip.

White told reporters during a roundtable at the Air, Space & Cyber conference that the restructuring process is nearing completion.

“We’re still on track for Milestone B. … That is going very well,” White said. “That was one of the areas I had concern early on about how you kind of navigate those waters and make sure you get that recertification right.”

Sentinel first received a Milestone B certification in 2020, but officials found over time that some of their baseline assumptions were no longer accurate.

The ground facilities in particular were the source of most of the problems rather than the missile itself. Those led to some “hard conversations” during the restructuring, White acknowledged, but senior leaders have now “pretty much locked down the majority of the design” for the infrastructure.

As part of that process, officials agreed Sentinel will no longer use the same silos as the Minuteman III, which are already around 60 years old. In March, the Air Force and Northrop broke ground on a new prototype silo in Promontory, Utah.

Broadly speaking, White said, the Air Force now has a better handle on the program as it progresses toward Milestone B once more.

“In terms of the cost piece, we’re learning as we go along because of just the sheer amount of data that we have now,” he said. “It’s so much more mature than when we did this [six] years ago, and so it’s been really fantastic, because we’ve integrated both the Air Force Cost Analysis Agency and [the office of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation] with us, and we’re going through this together.”

White declined to say what the restructured program may cost. The previous baseline from 2020 was $77.7 billion; officials said in 2024 it would be closer to $141 billion. White has said he is treating the latter as a cap on the program’s cost.

“I don’t think we’re anywhere near a number right now,” White said Sept. 14. “I’m very comfortable with what I have seen, though, and I think that we’re certainly within the realm of what we have talked about all along. So I don’t think you’ll see any surprises from a cost perspective.”

items.title: Department of War Announces Industry Participants in Falcon Peak 26.2
items.author: LTC Adam Scher
items.summary: The Department of War today announced the industry participants supporting Falcon Peak 26.2, a U.S. Northern Command and Joint Interagency Task Force 401 counter-small unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) experiment being conducted at Yuma Proving Ground from Aug. 31 through Sept. 25.
items.body:
The Department of War today announced the industry participants supporting Falcon Peak 26.2, a U.S. Northern Command and Joint Interagency Task Force 401 counter-small unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) experiment being conducted at Yuma Proving Ground from Aug. 31 through Sept. 25.

Falcon Peak 26.2 is the fourth operational evaluation in the series and the first conducted at Yuma Proving Ground. The experiment is designed to demonstrate new technologies, expand focus on low-collateral c-UAS defeat capabilities, collaborate with key partners, and provide immediate feedback to accelerate development of c-UAS solutions across the Department of War. This iteration of Falcon Peak targets the specific, complex C-UAS challenges unique to the Southern Border. ( Northcom )

The companies bring a range of capabilities spanning sensing, detection and tracking, artificial intelligence, command and control, semi-autonomous systems, airborne platforms and low-collateral defeat technologies. These capabilities are part of a layered defense, pairing top-tier technology with adequate training, tools, and permissions to effectively counter drone threats at the Southern Border and at installations across the country.

“Falcon Peak is about moving with urgency against the rapidly evolving drone threat,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401. “We are giving industry the opportunity to put innovative technologies in the hands of operators, test them against realistic threats and get immediate feedback on what works, what does not and what needs to change. Our objective is simple: quickly getting the right capabilities in the hand of warfighters to protect our installations and the Southern Border.”

items.title: Wilsbach Shares Airmen’s Stories of Epic Fury, Says 10 Got Battlefield Promotions for DUDE 44 Rescue
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: Ten Airmen received battlefield promotions for their roles in the daring rescue of DUDE 44, the crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle that was shot down over Iran this spring, Air Force Chief of Staff Ken. S. Wilsbach announced Sept. 14. Wilsbach revealed the promotions—a rarity in the Air Force—and more details about Airmen’s actions during Operation Epic Fury in a keynote address at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. The post Wilsbach Shares Airmen’s Stories of Epic Fury, Say
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —Ten Airmen received battlefield promotions for their roles in the daring rescue of DUDE 44, the crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle that was shot down over Iran this spring, Air Force Chief of Staff Ken. S. Wilsbach announced Sept. 14.

Wilsbach revealed the promotions—a rarity in the Air Force—and more details about Airmen’s actions during Operation Epic Fury in a keynote address at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.

Over the course of Epic Fury, which lasted from Feb. 28 until a shaky ceasefire in early April, the U.S. struck more than 13,000 military targets. In what was the biggest air campaign in a generation , around 500 combat aircraft executed around 250 sorties per day—10,000 sorties in 38 days, Wilsbach said.

American air bases in the Middle East went under “Alarm Red” conditions to take shelter, meaning there was an imminent threat of danger, 1,200 times. Wilsbach also said there were 48 airfield repairs and 420 “long lonely sweeps” to ensure that explosive ordnance was not left on the runway.

“That walk is exactly what the name suggests: one EOD technician, leaving a place of relative safety and approaching a suspected bomb or unexploded munition to render it safe for everyone else,” the chief said.

DUDE 44

Amid all these high-risk operations, the rescue of DUDE 44 in early April stood out as an example of the lengths the U.S. military was willing to go to save its service members.

In a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who was commander of Air Forces Central and the Combined Forces Air Component Commander for U.S. Central Command at the time of the mission and helped oversee the effort, said the rescue was one of his proudest moments in command.

“Watching 44 Bravo [the F-15E weapon systems officer] and getting the word that he was going to make it home and out of Iran with all the forces that were involved in that, knowing on Easter morning this guy was going to go see his family and call his wife for the first time in 48 hours was a high point, an emotional point for me having gone through that whole ordeal for the past 40-plus hours, and then recognized that we had got a win and got this guy back to safety,” France said.

For his part, Wilsbach singled out a particular battle manager—call sign “Peaches”—who coordinated the extraordinary search-and-rescue operation over 50 hours. To rescue the two-man crew, she and her team integrated the operations of 176 aircraft, including fighters, bombers, tankers, intelligence platforms, and special operations forces.

“Think about the complexity of that problem,” Wilsbach said. “Aircraft operating at different speeds, altitudes, fuel states, with different sensors, weapons, and responsibilities, while an adversary was actively trying to stop them.”

And that team was just part of the effort. Maintenance teams, Wilsbach said, generated additional fighters while tanker crews extended the force’s range and dwell time, and intelligence Airmen tracked threats.

“Every one of those Airmen was doing something different, yet all were contributing to the same mission,” Wilsbach said. That led to the 10 battlefield promotions, a rare occurrence when enlisted personnel are promoted for extraordinary performance of duties while serving in combat or under combat conditions.

“I had the distinct honor of promoting six of those heroes, ranging from staff sergeant to chief master sergeant, during a recent trip,’ Wilsbach said.

The dramatic rescue of the DUDE 44 crew began after an Iranian heat-seeking surface-to-air missile slammed into the two-seater fighter aircraft. Both crew members ejected. The pilot was rescued on the first day by a force that included A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, HC-130 Combat King IIs, HH-60W July Green II rescue helicopters, drones, and special warfare Airmen. That rescue operation was executed under close-range gunfire.

But the WSO, dubbed DUDE 44 Bravo, was not rescued for another day. He was injured in the fall, hitting the ground at a speed of 70 to 100 miles per hour after he struggled to unfurl a damaged parachute, according to an interview he gave to the CBS News program “60 Minutes.”

After landing five miles away from the pilot, DUDE 44 Bravo was suffering from a broken back, a broken arm, a broken shoulder, a sprained ankle, and cuts to his head and face. To elude capture, he scaled a 7,000-foot-tall ridgeline.

Airmen in Epic Fury

Wilsbach cited the work of Airmen across Epic Fury to emphasize his main directives for the service: be “ready to fight, built to endure, and integrated to win.”

The rescue of DUDE 44 was a prime example of integration, the chief said.

To illustrate readiness to fight, Wilsbach told the story of an unnamed base under attack from Iranian missiles.

“As missiles were inbound, Airmen sprinted toward bunkers,” Wilsbach said. “A missile struck nearby in a hangar, and the aircraft inside burst into flames. The bunker withstood the blast, but the force of the impact damaged the door so badly it wouldn’t open, trapping the Airmen inside.”

A security forces NCO used a pry bar to force the door partially open and spoke with the Airmen inside. But then the ejection seat on the burning aircraft ignited, “sending glass and metal fragments through the air,” Wilsbach said. At last, the Airmen were able to get the door open and run for cover. Finally, the door gave way, and the Airmen ran for cover.

Wilsbach also shared the story of an F-15E crew chief, Garrett, who stayed with the jets on the flight line until the last F-15E taxied and took off while others were running for cover. “ When somebody later asked him why, his answer was simple: they needed those airplanes in the air,” Wilsbach said.

Hundreds of miles away, two Senior Airmen, Shanea and Nolan, tracked a swarm of enemy drones headed toward their base and, Wilbach said, achieved more than 10 surface-to-air kills.

Shanea and Nolan’s actions in particular show the need for the Air Force to advance point defense and make it a “core function of air and space power,” Wilsbach said; the Air Force can no longer be assured that it is safe from drone and missile threats, including at airfields in the United States.

“Don’t you think we ought to have them at every base?” Wilsbach said of a new field of Airmen specializing in point defense. “If every base is going to be threatened, we have to have somebody who knows how to defend it.

“If we had a more robust base defense, you know, perhaps those bases wouldn’t have been as damaged as they were,” Wilsbach added. “Look at Israel; they have a significantly layered, very robust defense of their country, and they didn’t take that many hits, very few, in fact. And that shows you what a good defensive system can do, which can help you to operate not quite with impunity, but almost, and you can just keep generating airpower, and your defensive systems take care of the incoming.”

To hammer home his point about endurance, Wilsbach told the store of a a B-1 pilot, with the call sign Rocket, who coped with a harrowing refueling at night, in heavy clouds, and with jet fuel spraying across his cockpit windscreen.

The B-1 crew described the experience as “refueling by Braille,” Wilsbach said.

“A bomber pilot who couldn’t see depended on the tanker crew to guide them,” Wilsbach added, noting that the B-1 went on to complete a 34-hour mission.

Another example, the chief said, was an MQ-9 pilot, call sign Suit, who launched his drone while its airfield was under attack. The drone struck a target, then returned to base to conduct a damage assessment of the runway. That mission was one of many the MQ-9 conducted during Epic Fury, Wilsbach noted, with a remotely piloted aircraft striking more than 800 targets. It also played a key role in dynamic targeting and locations where the U.S. did not want to operate crewed aircraft. “Many more targets were hit because the MQ-9 found them and then passed them off to another platform,” Wilsbach said. “There’s a lot more than the 800 that they hit, and we were doing this in areas that were highly defended. And though we did decimate the Iranian Air Force and the Iranian Navy, and then we significantly attrited other capabilities that they have, it wasn’t easy. Iran’s not a pushover.”

items.title: US Air Force secretary reveals deployment of on-orbit space control weapons
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink revealed that the service deployed on-orbit space control weapons but did not offer details on the type of weapon.
items.body:
Space

US Air Force secretary reveals deployment of on-orbit space control weapons

Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink announced the on-orbit space control weapons during a keynote address at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference. (EJ Hersom/U.S. Defense Department)

The U.S. Department of the Air Force deployed on-orbit space control weapons in an effort to meet evolving threats from adversaries and boost space capabilities .

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink announced Monday at the the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference that the service has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against “hostile adversary action.”

Meink announced in a keynote address Monday at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference that the service has on-orbit space control weapons that are capable of defending the joint force against “hostile adversary action.”

Meink offered no other details, saying only that the phrasing was “well thought out.” He said maintaining and being able to depend on U.S. space capabilities is necessary as adversaries develop their own capabilities to threaten them.

“It is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space, and so that we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that,” he said during his speech.

During a media roundtable following the keynote, Meink declined to comment on the type of weapons or why the announcement was made now.

Meink’s statement is the most direct public acknowledgment by a U.S. official to date regarding space control weapons, but he did not say when the weapons were launched or how many are in orbit.

Meink said that for more than a decade, the U.S. has been aware that adversaries such as China and Russia were developing their own capabilities to threaten U.S. systems.

“We need to maintain dominance in space as it becomes more and more important to how we function, how we operate militarily and economically, civilian-wise,” he told reporters.

The secretary called it necessary for deterrence, but he would not give more details about the weapons, saying that would negate its purpose.

“I’m not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested or not tested or anything else,” he said.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

items.title: PAE(A), industry partner to deliver hypersonic missile technology
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: The Navy has awarded industry partner Castelion a Small Business Innovation Research Phase III production contract worth up to $200 million for the Blackbeard hypersonic missile. This air-launched, high-speed strike weapon will equip carrier-based strike fighters, significantly expanding their lethal reach and survivability against advanced defenses. By leveraging commercial manufacturing and agile acquisition reforms, this landmark program rapidly delivers "affordable mass" and high-speed deter
items.body:
PORTFOLIO ACQUISTION EXECUTIVE AVIATION, PATUXENT RIVER, Md. – The Navy took another step forward today to extend the operational reach of Carrier Strike Groups and existing aviation platforms with cost-effective, scalable systems through a Small Business Innovation Research Phase III production delivery order for the Blackbeard hypersonic missile, total value up to $200 million. Awarded by Portfolio Acquisition Executive Aviation (PAE(A)) through its Future Capability Development and Integration (FCD&I) Aviation Rapid Capabilities Cell and in collaboration with Naval Air Warfare Centers, the contract is an example of how private-public partnerships can advance production capabilities to achieve warfighting goals.

Developed by industry partner Castelion, Blackbeard is an air-launched, hypersonic strike weapon that provides carrier-based strike fighters with a responsive, long-range, high-speed strike option against maritime and land targets, enhancing survivability against advanced air defenses while significantly increasing magazine depth. The award supports naval aviation’s response to the call in the National Defense Strategy mandate to build a resilient, competitive industrial base. It also satisfies the National Security Strategy priority for high-speed deterrence in contested maritime regions and addresses the Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle's "Foundry Always" directive for affordable munitions at scale.

Castelion will manufacture, assemble, test and deliver the initial lot of Blackbeard Hypersonic Weapon All-Up Rounds, providing naval aviation with an affordable, rapidly fieldable and highly survivable long-range strike capability. By leveraging advanced commercial manufacturing methods and a vertically integrated production line, this landmark program introduces immediate "affordable mass" to the fleet—a critical requirement under the Department of the Navy's Hedge Strategy and Commander, Naval Air Forces Vice Adm. Doug Verissimo’s (“Air Boss”) operational readiness goals.

“To win in contested environments, we must deliver lethality at scale inside the operational window of relevance,” said Vice Adm. John “Doc” Dougherty IV, commander PAE(A) and Naval Air Systems Command. “This production award is a testament to what is possible when the Navy aligns agile acquisition with commercial manufacturing discipline. We are putting game-changing hypersonic capability into the hands of our warfighters, dramatically expanding the lethal reach of naval aviation.”

This award leverages Congressional acquisition reform in the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, using the Small Business Innovation Development Act to rapidly transition successful technology developed through private capital investment directly into production. This approach reduces millions of dollars in redundant, non-recurring engineering costs while introducing aggressive commercial competition into the munitions production ecosystem.

To ensure seamless integration and total mission assurance, the Blackbeard weapon system leverages mission engineering rigor and innovative testing software developed by Silicon Valley. This modern testing approach guarantees that the advanced tactical rounds meet the Navy’s rigorous flight clearance and safety standards, paving the way for rapid and reliable deployment.

Contact the PAE(A) Public Affairs Office regarding Blackbeard or PAE(A) rapid transition initiatives.

items.title: Oregon National Guard uses new hoist technology in live mountain rescue
items.author: MAJ Wayne Clyne
items.summary: An Oregon Army National Guard aircrew used a new self-stabilizing hoist device in one of the first live rescues of its kind Sept. 12, helping locate and extract an injured hunter from the remote Mount Jefferson Wilderness. The device, which the crew calls the Vita, stabilizes a rescue litter during hoist operations without requiring a ground medic or tagline, letting crews reach terrain previously out of range. The mission marked one of the technology's first operational successes following more
items.body:
SALEM, Ore., a new self-stabilizing hoist device helped an Oregon Army National Guard aircrew rescue an injured hunter from the Mount Jefferson Wilderness Sept. 12, marking one of the first live operational uses of the technology in the country.

A pair of hunters were roughly 10 miles from the nearest road when one of them slipped and broke an ankle. With few options to call for help, the hunters improvised, tying a piece of orange and white clothing to a pole and spinning it to catch the attention of the air crew overhead.

"They had fashioned a signaling device with orange and white, I don't know if it was articles of clothing, but put that on a pole and spun it, which created a signaling device that allowed us to locate them," said Chief Warrant Officer 3 Noelan Smith.

Smith, Staff Sgt. Michael Lam and three other crew members were finishing another flight in an HH-60M Black Hawk helicopter from Golf Company, 1st Battalion, 189th Aviation Regiment, when they were redirected to the scene. The Oregon Department of Emergency Management requested the Guard's help after the hunters used a satellite communication device to call for a rescue.

Instead of the traditional method of hoisting a litter, in which a medic on the ground steadies the basket with a tagline as it's lowered and raised, the crew relied on the new device for one of the first times in a real-world rescue. The system, which the crew calls the Vita, attaches to the rescue basket and uses fans to counteract wind and other forces that can cause the basket to spin during a hoist.

"Under normal circumstances, there'd be a medic on the ground using what we call a tagline, a rope attached to the basket, which lets it so it doesn't spin. But with this Vita that we attach to our rescue basket, we don't have to have a tagline anymore and it just stabilizes it up the whole time," said Lam, who operated the device during the rescue while Smith flew the aircraft.

The Oregon National Guard first began testing the technology in June 2025, when a team of Guard flight medics worked with Army researchers in Salem to help shape the design of a next-generation medevac aircraft. Oregon was selected for the testing in part because of its steep, forested and often snow-covered terrain, which regularly pushes rescue crews to the edge of what current aircraft and equipment can safely do.

The litter attachment uses an electric propulsion system to counteract spin, bringing a rotating basket back under control in a matter of seconds, and a thrust-vectoring system that reads its own orientation many times per second to hold or adjust the basket's heading even in heavy rotor wash. A wireless handheld control lets a crew member direct the litter's rotation and toggle it between standby and active modes from well outside the aircraft, without needing a ground crew or a tagline to steady it.

Saturday's rescue put that research to work in the field. Smith said the device's ability to keep a litter steady without a ground medic opens up terrain that was previously out of reach.

"If it's cliffside, things like that, we don't necessarily have the ability to have somebody on the ground and move the aircraft in a manner that we'd be able to use a traditional basket with tagline. So this provides us a resource that can get into those spaces that we wouldn't be able to in the past," Smith said.

The injured hunter was flown to a hospital and received treatment within a few hours of the rescue. Guard officials said it was among the technology's first operational successes and that it could eventually be fielded beyond Oregon.

Oregon National Guard aviators fly several search-and-rescue and medevac missions each year, supporting county sheriff's offices and the Oregon Department of Emergency Management across the state's mountains, deserts and coastline.

items.title: Exercise Ultimate Caduceus 2026: global patient movement enterprise
items.author: SrA Jordan Lazaro
items.summary: Approximately 400 military and civilian personnel gathered to reinforce a shared commitment to patient-centered care during Exercise Ultimate Caduceus 2026 held Sept. 2-12, 2026, at Scott AFB.
items.body:
SCOTT AIR FORCE BASE, Ill. – Approximately 400 military and civilian personnel gathered to reinforce a shared commitment to patient-centered care during Exercise Ultimate Caduceus 2026 held Sept. 2-12, 2026, at Scott AFB.

The annual patient movement field training exercise, led by U.S. Transportation Command, simulates receiving injured troops from overseas locations at designated aeromedical evacuation hubs and patient reception areas where federal coordinating centers and local partners receive, triage, stage, track and transport patients to pre-designated local definitive care facilities.

“Ultimate Caduceus is about the power of our partnership and a testament to our nation’s shared commitment to providing world-class care,” said Air Force Col. Christopher Backus, USTRANSCOM command surgeon. “The synergy between our military medical teams and the incredible expertise of our community and interagency partners creates a resilient network that is greater than the sum of its parts. Together, we are ready for any crisis.”

The exercise kicked off with hands-on training evaluating the readiness of the patient movement enterprise. Participants were assessed on their ability to scale up forces and deploy sufficient medical assets to provide expedited transport of military patients to locations within the United States for care within a collective effort with our military and industry partners.

“Opportunities like this are crucial for our soldiers to come out and flex their medical skill sets not only with our military, but with industry partners,” said Army Maj. Jesse Back, 7450th Medical Operational Readiness Unit officer in charge of the patient insertion team. “Testing our real-world abilities and interoperability away from our home station only makes for a stronger united warfighting team.”

A central focus of this exercise was testing the aeromedical evacuation mission, which provides time-sensitive, fixed-wing, critical in-flight care to patients in transit from locations overseas to the United States. Global operations depend on the medical enterprises ability to project, maneuver and sustain the joint force and are made stronger through continued relationships with our partners and allies.

“Working directly with other services builds trust by helping us understand each other’s capabilities and work through challenges before we have to do it in a real-world operation,” said Air Force Maj. Melissa Cadorette, Air Mobility Command A37 Joint Exercise Division exercise support branch chief. “While this exercise is focused on joint integration across the medical field, my biggest takeaway has been seeing how important communication and coordination are across all organizations involved in patient movement.”

Multiple aircraft were involved to make this exercise possible. Air Force C-130J Super Hercules, Army C-12 Huron, Army HH-60 Black Hawks and civilian cargo and passenger aircraft participated, allowing joint and civilian medical teams to train on a variety of airlift platforms. This global patient enterprise provides safe, reliable and scalable patient movement for the Department of War.

“Commercial patient movement services are centered around individual patients,” said Anthony Ross, U.S. Transportation Command Defense Health Agency liaison officer. “Ultimate Caduceus provides an opportunity to strengthen our public-private partnerships, test and integrate high-volume commercial capabilities and scale the War Department’s capacity to deliver warfighters from the battlefield to care.”

Readiness is a shared responsibility. UC26 is where our community of experts come together to share insight and refine a collective approach to patient care. The exercise is an opportunity to strengthen our integration, test our readiness and ensure our robust network is prepared for any crisis.

“Through joint training and collaboration, participants gain a better understanding of each organization’s capabilities, procedures and challenges,” said Army Reserve Lt. Col. David Stefl, 807th Theater Medical Command joint task force medical deputy commander. “The success in future operations depends not only on individual technical proficiency, but also on the ability to integrate with partners. Through this exercise we build on these relationships to enhance readiness, improve patient care in operational environments and increase our collective ability to respond effectively when called upon.”

USTRANSCOM’s role is to integrate efforts with interagency partners to create a seamless community of care. Together, we can move every patient safely and efficiently to the definitive medical care they need anywhere within the United States.

“Federal and industry partners expand War Department medical capacity – testing our interoperability at Ultimate Caduceus increases our readiness to deliver warfighters from the battlefield to the DHA, TRICARE, VA and HHS healthcare networks,” said William Walker, Defense Health Agency assistant director of healthcare administration and operations. “Building this foundation now positions War Department leaders to rapidly integrate and scale federal and industry capacity to meet our nation’s warfighting requirements.”

Exercises like Ultimate Caduceus increase interoperability across medical teams and systems so we can provide the highest level of care for those who need it most. Additionally, it reinforced the importance of preparedness for future conflict and DHA’s sacred obligation to provide lifesaving care on and off the battlefield.

items.title: ‘It’s not science fiction’: US Air Force must build trust in AI, says expert
items.author: Claire Barrett
items.summary: The military must work on how to combat fast and reckless enemy AI agents that don’t necessarily operate with the same oversight, according to experts.
items.body:
Air Warfare

‘It’s not science fiction’: US Air Force must build trust in AI, says expert

Tacet Venari participants analyze metadata to identify any suspicious activity on the network during exercise Tacet Venari at Ramstein Air Base, Germany, May 12, 2022. (U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Jared Lovett)

Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation has underscored growing concerns about the risks posed by AI. Coxon said that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Michael Hiatt, chief technology officer of Epirus, has taken a different tack.

During a panel regarding counter-drone defenses at the Air and Space Cyber Conference, Hiatt noted that “everyone talks about cost asymmetry… and how important that solving that cost asymmetry problem is. But for the folks that are on the ground, the battle captain trying to make that assessment, it’s not a cost asymmetry problem. It’s a magazine doubt issue.”

“When you have a problem like UAS threats, they’re coming in mass,” Hiatt continued. Trust in an airman’s system, he emphasized, is crucial when the threat time has been cut down to seconds.

“I know that my DE [Directed Energy] weapons are gonna be able to take it out, and do so in a low-collateral way, in a very low cost per shot way, and most importantly, in a way that preserves my magazine — my scarce interceptors, and then they’ll be able to push that button.”

The challenge, according to Hiatt, is “putting that work in and building that trust. It’s not science fiction. It’s physics fact.”

For Hiatt, utilizing AI in counter-drone defense is a tool with humans initially “in the loop” but ultimately working towards a system where humans start the loop and then end up on the outside of the operating system. However, building that trust amid an industry that is still formulating its own AI policy regulations is difficult, the panelists concede.

But despite this, the panelists argue, the proverbial cat is out of the bag regarding artificial intelligence, and the U.S. military must work on how to combat fast and reckless enemy AI agents that don’t necessarily operate with the same oversight.

The military must continue “to evolve, because the threat is evolving,” said panelist Colton Wood, chief technology officer of Digital Force Technologies. “And if we don’t evolve our defenses to basically counter that, we’re just gonna always be on our heels.

Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.

items.author: SGT Danielle Rayon

items.body:
CAMP GRUBER TRAINING CENTER, Okla. — Oklahoma National Guard Soldiers put their tactics, techniques and procedures to the test during Exercise Thunderstruck 3.0, an unmanned systems-centered exercise held at Camp Gruber Training Center, Sept. 12, 2026.

This year’s iteration of the annual exercise trained Oklahoma National Guard members against evolving threats, while military representatives from other states, international partners and industry representatives observed scenarios incorporating unmanned aerial systems and other emerging capabilities.

“It’s trying to mold all of that into one operation so that we can test our systems, we can test our tactics, our techniques and our procedures to figure out what works, what doesn’t work, and then focus on what doesn’t work,” said Brig. Gen. Colby Wyatt, director of the joint staff for Oklahoma National Guard.

The training reflects lessons from modern battlefields, where rapidly evolving unmanned systems provide persistent surveillance, track troop movements and influence how military formations maneuver.

“We have a dedicated exercise to take the emerging technology, put it in the hands of Soldiers and let them execute in a controlled environment where we can go back in and look at what we did and make sure what we’re doing is the right thing,” said Maj. Michael Horn, commander, 1st Battalion, 179th Infantry Regiment, 45th Infantry Brigade Combat Team.

That complexity also puts greater demands on junior leaders.

“It takes a lot of training,” Horn said. “It takes a lot of learning for that leader on the ground to be able to understand the capabilities of the systems within his formation and how to employ them effectively to both protect and survive on the battlefield and be lethal.”

This year’s training incorporated UH-60 Black Hawk operations, tactical convoy movements, medical evacuation (MEDEVAC) operations and UAS capabilities, giving participants opportunities to rehearse how they would operate, communicate and maneuver while facing threats from the air and ground.

“Exercise Thunderstruck helps the National Guard to get after their dual-use mission of domestic response and tactical-edge warfighting capability with drones, helicopters, other effects and fixed-wing aircraft safely, and teaching the young Soldiers and leaders in our environment how to be competitive and what the next fight looks like,” said retired Col. Shane Riley, co-owner of RXR Worldwide, which supports the Oklahoma Military Department by developing innovation capabilities, partnerships and digital airspace awareness for exercises like Thunderstruck. Friendly and opposing UAS operated throughout the exercise, providing both battlefield capabilities and simulated threats.

“We’re deploying these drones out into the environment to enable the units to be more lethal, to have better communications, and have a better understanding of the battlefield around them,” Riley said. “And then we’re also doing threat replication with those drones to make them deal with what the facts would look like in their next conflict.”

That integration of capabilities and threats is central to Thunderstruck 3.0, which brings multiple systems and training scenarios together to test how units operate in a complex battlefield environment.

Thunderstruck is part of the Oklahoma National Guard’s broader effort to develop UAS and counter-UAS capabilities through the Launched Effects Program, which since 2022 has brought together military, industry, academic and government partners to address emerging technologies and threats.

“We have state partners, interagency partners, domestic response partners, industry that are looking for ways to be relevant in the dual-use space, both commercial domestic protection and military applications,” Riley said.

For Guard leaders, the objective of Thunderstruck is not simply to demonstrate new technology, but to give Soldiers an environment where they can experiment, identify weaknesses and refine how they operate before lives depend on it.

“We want to make sure that we set them up for success and we get them to start thinking about these different things, because they’re the ones on the ground,” said Col. Steve Cheadle, brigade commander for 90th Troop Command. “They’re the ones that are in harm’s way, and they’re the ones trying to lead their troops to make sure that they’re safe and they get back home.”

Exercise Thunderstruck 3.0 represents another step in the Oklahoma National Guard’s effort to keep pace with rapidly changing technology and ensure its formations are prepared to operate in an increasingly complex environment.

“You’re going to have to make some failures to find out where those gaps are in order to figure it out, to succeed,” Wyatt said. “The overarching goal of this is we want to protect our Soldiers better, for their survival on the battlefield.”

items.title: STARCOM highlights plan to deliver Space Force growth
items.author: Maj. Ryan DeCamp
items.summary: As the U.S. Space Force prepares to double its uniformed ranks over the next five years, Space Training and Readiness Command is setting the foundation to turn that historic expansion into ready, combat-credible space forces. Dr. Troy Meink, secretary of the Air Force, said during a keynote address Sept. 14 at the Air and Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space and Cyber Conference the military must rapidly field cost-effective combat power to keep pace with a modern technological revolution.
items.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. — As the U.S. Space Force prepares to double its uniformed ranks over the next five years, Space Training and Readiness Command is setting the foundation to turn that historic expansion into ready, combat-credible space forces.

Dr. Troy Meink, secretary of the Air Force, said during a keynote address Sept. 14 at the Air and Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space and Cyber Conference the military must rapidly field cost-effective combat power to keep pace with a modern technological revolution. Meink emphasized service members are the foundation of this adaptability, noting the growth of the Space Force is a direct reflection of that investment in personnel.

Maj. Gen. James E. Smith, STARCOM commander, outlined how the command will drive this growth during his media roundtable and the Growth of the Space Force panel at the conference.

“We understand the requirements behind right-sizing the Space Force, and we are fully postured to meet those goals for FY27,” Smith said. “Adding 10,000 Guardians over the next five years represents our target, with a significant portion of that growth occurring in the first year. Predictable budget resources will remain vital as we scale operations to maintain our FY27 momentum.”

Doubling the service is more than recruiting and classroom throughput; it requires experienced warfighters stepping forward to shape the force. STARCOM is actively seeking more than 200 Guardians and civilian specialists to fill vital instructor roles across officer and enlisted basic training, commissioning pipelines, initial skills training and professional military education.

The assignment demand distributes Guardian instructors to Air Force ROTC detachments nationwide, Officer Training School, located at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama, and the U.S. Air Force Academy, in Colorado Springs, Colorado. An increase in instructors will also support three enlisted initial skills training locations and the enlisted PME courses.

Smith emphasized that serving as an instructor or educator at STARCOM represents a foundational assignment for the service, helping create a deliberate pathway for Guardians to develop warfighting acumen, exercise mission command and advance toward mastery.

“Our success hinges entirely on our people, and recruiting top talent into instructor billets creates the combat credibility our service needs,” Smith said. “STARCOM is the crucible where Guardians are shaped and systems are proven. When experienced operators step into instructor assignments, they directly instill the space warfighting ethos that our joint force depends upon.”

Absorbing the growth

STARCOM will have to onboard and qualify these cadre members rapidly to handle an incoming surge in students. In fiscal 2027, STARCOM plans to expand its Basic Military Training pipeline, located at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, by more than 90% to accommodate over 1,400 recruits, with subsequent initial skills courses expanding at a matching rate. Enlisted professional military education will grow by nearly 120% to train more than 1,300 students annually.

Officer accession programs will experience similar demands. OTS will scale its pipeline by nearly 600% to prepare roughly 850 Guardian officer trainees, while Air Force ROTC expects to commission approximately 300 Guardians next year, a 100% jump.

Following commissioning, new officers enter the comprehensive Officer Training Course, located at Peterson Space Force Base, Colorado, where enrollment will jump roughly 275% to more than 1,350 officers next fiscal year. Officer professional military education will eventually absorb an additional 1,600 students, representing a 330% increase.

Cultivating collaboration, purpose-built facilities

Meeting this rapid demand also accelerates STARCOM’s push for service-tailored, Guardian unique development opportunities designed specifically for space domain challenges.

“The Marine Corps operates within the Department of the Navy, yet both services recognize that Marines require distinct training and development from Sailors,” Smith said. “The same holds true within the Department of the Air Force.

“While we currently have a great partnership with the US Air Force for many of our development courses,” he continued, “ultimately, Guardians require space-minded education and rigorous, domain-specific training to ensure combat credibility, integrate seamlessly with the joint force and protect national interests.”

STARCOM already leverages deliberate partnerships to accelerate Guardian-unique development. In January, STARCOM and Space Delta 13 partnered with Texas A&M University in College Station, Texas, to launch the Captains Leadership Course, pairing active-duty Guardian instructors with university faculty. The program has graduated more than 270 Guardians, and the Space Force recently finalized a 10-year intergovernmental support agreement to sustain the partnership through 2036.

Smith highlighted this academic alliance as a model for how STARCOM cultivates a collaborative culture across the military, industry and academia.

“Every American relies daily on space-enabled capabilities, which means our joint and coalition forces must possess the ability to operate in, from, and to space at a time and place of their choosing,” Smith said. “STARCOM touches every Guardian’s career, either in the classroom or through the operational systems and tactics we validate.

“By building positive partnerships, bolstering our development foundation, and setting high standards in our schoolhouses,” he continued, “we will continue forging the world’s most combat-credible Space Force.”

items.title: Fort Riley sergeant sentenced to 31 years in prison for child rape
items.author: Michelle McCaskill
items.summary: An Army sergeant who pleaded guilty to raping a child was sentenced by the military judge to 31 years in prison during his court-martial Sept. 4 at the Fort Riley courtroom. Staff Sgt. Rodney S. Sneed III, 35, an M1 Armor Crewmember assigned to the 4th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Infantry Division, was also sentenced to a dishonorable discharge from the Army.
items.body:
FORT RILEY, Kan. – An Army sergeant who pleaded guilty to raping a child was sentenced by the military judge to 31 years in prison during his court-martial Sept. 4 at the Fort Riley courtroom.

Staff Sgt. Rodney S. Sneed III, 35, an M1 Armor Crewmember assigned to the 4th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Infantry Division, was also sentenced to a dishonorable discharge from the Army.

On Sept. 12, 2025, the victim, an 11-year-old, confided to a friend that Sneed raped her the previous day.

The friend notified a school guidance counselor who reported the incident to the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division.

Army CID agents spoke to the victim briefly at the school, then transported her to their offices for a more extensive interview where she informed them that Sneed repeatedly raped her over the years.

After the interview, Army CID agents accompanied her off post to the hospital in Manhattan, Kansas, where evidence collected during a Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Exam confirmed she had been sexually assaulted by Sneed.

“This result would not have been possible without the immense bravery of the victim in coming forward, the hard work of Army CID’s Fort Riley Resident Agency, and the dogged pursuit of justice by the prosecution team,” said Maj. Bryanna Beauchamp, Special Trial Counsel Officer In Charge, Fort Riley Field Office, Army Office of Special Trial Counsel.

“Army CID remains unwavering in its commitment to pursuing anyone who harms, exploits, or abuses a child,” said Special Agent in Charge Derek Tilton, Army CID’s Central Field Office. “While no punishment can undo the suffering endured by the victim, this outcome delivers meaningful accountability for an act of profound cruelty.”

Sneed will serve his confinement at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Upon release from prison, he will be required to register as a sex offender under federal and state statutory requirements.

This case was investigated by Army CID’s Fort Riley Resident Agency, and prosecuted by Capt. Kelsey Constantino, Fourth Circuit, Fort Riley Field Office, Army OSTC, and Capt. Steve Hollins, Office of the Staff Judge Advocate, 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Infantry Division.

About the Army Office of Special Trial Counsel: The Army Office of Special Trial Counsel is composed of specially trained military lawyers, legal professionals and support staff responsible for the expert prosecution of murder, sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse, kidnapping and other serious criminal offenses. Headquartered at Fort Belvoir, Va., OSTC has eight regional headquarters that oversee 28 field offices located worldwide, including locations in Europe and Korea. For more information visit http://www.army.mil/ostc.

To Report a Crime: If you would like to report a crime, have information about a crime, or have been the subject or survivor of a crime, you can submit anonymous tips to Army CID at http://www.p3tips.com/armycid.

FORT LEE, Va. – The U.S. Army Transportation Command Executive Director visited U.S. Army Combined Arms Support Command Sept. 14 to discuss ARTRANS role in contested logistics, watercraft and integration with CASCOM. Kristina O’Brien leads ARTRANS, the Army service component command to U.S. Transportation Command, and a major subordinate command to Army Materiel Command. ARTRANS provides deployment and distribution capabilities to meet national objectives. During her visit, O’Brien met with leadership from CASCOM and the U.S. Army Transportation Corps and Transportation School. She also spoke to the students attending the Joint Logistics Course at Army Sustainment University. ARTRANS connects and synchronizes surface warfighting requirements through distribution network nodes to the point of need, responsively projecting power and delivering desired effects in support of combatant commands and the Total Joint Force. The command also partners with the commercial transportation industry as the coordinating link between Department of War surface transportation requirements and the capability industry provides.

items.body: On Sept. 11, 2026, the White Sands Missile Range community gathered under the banner of “WSMR NEVER FORGET,” united in solemn remembrance of the lives lost on September 11, 2001. From first light, a powerful sense of reflection and solidarity filled the air as service members, first responders, families, and civilians came together to pay tribute. The weight of memory was ever-present, with many attendees recalling exactly where they were on that fateful morning, forging a shared bond of resilience and honor. From the earliest moments of this somber day, leadership stood shoulder to shoulder with the community, offering support and solidarity. WSMR Garrison Commander Col. Michael Lueckeman not only attended but also served as the guest speaker at New Mexico State University’s 9/11 Memorial Stair Climb and Ceremony at Aggie Memorial Stadium. His participation highlighted WSMR's commitment to honoring the legacy of 9/11 alongside the Las Cruces community. At the Headquarters Building, a poignant flag-raising ceremony unfolded, joining the WSMR Fire Department and soldiers in solemn tribute. Together, they honored the memory of those lost on 9/11, standing in silent reverence as the flag was raised, a powerful reminder of the day’s significance. A solemn Remembrance Ceremony at the Post Chapel brought together service members, community members, and civilians, united by shared respect, grief, and resolve. Lueckeman delivered a moving speech that resonated deeply with all in attendance, reflecting on the enduring impact of 9/11. The ceremony culminated with the WSMR Fire and Police Departments performing a powerful final call tribute for 9/11, followed by the playing of taps, a stirring reminder of the sacrifices made and the unwavering spirit of first responders. Afterward, the community moved to the Frontier Club for a special lunch honoring fire, police, and first responders. The lunch was a gesture of gratitude, open to all, and filled with stories of bravery and sacrifice. Towards the end of the workday, the WSMR community assembled once more for the 9/11 Stair Climb at the LC32 Gantry. Participants, from seasoned service members to young dependents, climbed in remembrance of the firefighters who made the ultimate sacrifice. Every step was a tribute, every breath a reminder that the legacy of 9/11 continues to inspire courage and unity. Through these acts of remembrance, the WSMR community ensured that 9/11 would always be a day of reflection, honor, and resilience, a day that would never be erased from memory.

items.title: Corpus Christi Army Depot completes historic Chinook maintenance milestone
items.author: Kathleen Pettaway-Clarke
items.summary: Corpus Christi Army Depot reached a milestone in August 2026, which marked the revitalization of CH-47F phase maintenance following a 15-year program hiatus. This critical depot-level maintenance directly enhances fleet readiness, ensuring immediate, reliable support to warfighters in the field.
items.body:
CORPUS CHRISTI ARMY DEPOT, Texas--- Corpus Christi Army Depot reached a milestone in August 2026, which marked the revitalization of CH-47F phase maintenance following a 15-year program hiatus. This critical depot-level maintenance directly enhances fleet readiness, ensuring immediate, reliable support to warfighters in the field.

CCAD is one of the Army’s Organic Industrial Base, which includes 23 depots, arsenals and ammunition plants, which manufacture and reset equipment, generating readiness and operational capability**.**

Structural Branch Chief Luis Gaitan said, “Our hope for this aircraft is to show the Army that we can provide them with a quality aircraft that meets their requirements, ready to fly and ready to go.”

The CH-47 Chinook is the U.S. Army’s sole heavy-lift helicopter and remains vital to both overseas contingency operations and homeland security. As a critical multi-mission asset, the Chinook transports troops and supplies while providing essential combat support and combat service support. Its versatile secondary capabilities include medical evacuation, aircraft recovery, disaster relief, and search and rescue.

Referring to the August success, John Scherer, branch chief for the CH-47 Assembly Department Disassembly Area said, “We were originally scheduled to meet our Gate 4 milestone in mid-September, but the team successfully completed the phase and delivered the aircraft ahead of schedule. “

The depot's long history of sustaining the CH-47 Chinook began in 1983 when the depot welcomed the CH-47D workload. This transition followed a comprehensive Department of Defense study on realigning the Army's aircraft maintenance missions, which recommended transferring the function from the New Cumberland Army Depot in Pennsylvania to CCAD in Texas.

Sustainment reached a major milestone on February 6, 2010, when CCAD delivered its first modernized CH-47F Chinook helicopter to Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. This delivery represented a major turning point in the depot's support of the global Chinook fleet, reinforcing CCAD's role in maintaining the Army's heavy-lift capabilities.

Under the Army Transformation Initiative, the U.S. Army pivoted to a new strategic plan that reduced the active helicopter fleet to fund modernization priorities. This structural shift ultimately decreased organic depot maintenance volume, directly impacting operations at CCAD as part of a broader force-wide realignment. Although the program was previously discontinued, the depot is re-establishing its capabilities to ensure warfighters have immediate access to mission-ready aircraft. The operational readiness program is tailored based on the Army’s needs and will build tactical unit readiness by providing depot-repaired equipment in conjunction with field maintenance training.

Upon the helicopter's arrival in December 2024, leadership assembled a highly experienced, cross-functional team from various departments to execute a targeted phase maintenance process rather than full recapitalization.

Speaking about the effort to recruit skilled artisans, Avionics Electrical Work Lead Dale Bower said, “We selected personnel from throughout the depot based on their previous experience with this aircraft, including specialists from our aircraft mechanic groups, electrical, and sheet metal teams.”

Bower continued, “We carefully canvassed the depot to identify experienced personnel before assembling the crew. Once the team was assigned, we initiated the disassembly and phase maintenance process.”

Referring to the challenges, Gaitan said, “Since this was the first CH‑47 we’ve worked on in a long time, getting every entity to support us was a challenge. For instance, obstacles included getting the program back on track, securing the support equipment, and tracking down many small parts.”

Gaitan said, “However, we successfully delivered ahead of schedule. It was a great success story for our structures team.”

Aircraft Electrician, Michael Escammila, Aviation Maintenance Group. highlighted the importance of the program for the depot, “The success of this program provides the potential to bring in more work and hire more employees.”

As a subject matter expert, Escammila, expressed confidence in the depot's efficiency and quality, especially with the new F models.

The Corpus Christi Army Depot achieved a major operational landmark by completing its first CH-47 Chinook phase maintenance initiative in 15 years. This achievement deepens CCAD’s integration into global Army operations and strengthens its long-term sustainment of the warfighter.
